# Online Graph Coloring with Random Arrivals Hirotaka Yoneda∗
The University of Tokyo, Japan
squar37@gmail.com Masataka Yoneda†
The University of Tokyo, Japan
e869120@gmail.com **Abstract** We study online graph coloring in the random-arrival model, where the vertices are presented in a uniformly random order. Assuming _n_ and _k_ are known in advance, we present a randomized exponential-time algorithm that colors any _k_-colorable graph on _n_ vertices with _O(k_3log2_k_log4_n_) colors in expectation. This is the first online coloring algorithm that uses a polylogarithmic number of colors for all fixed \(k\ge 3\), and is better than a known lower bound of \(\Omega(log^{k-1}n)\) colors under adversarial arrivals for all fixed \(k\ge 6\). In addition, assuming _n_ is known in advance, we obtain a competitive ratio of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\). For comparison, it is known to be NP-hard to approximate (offline) graph coloring within a factor of \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) for all fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Therefore, our exponential-time online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the NP-hardness threshold for polynomial-time approximation algorithms. ∗Supported by JSPS JP25K24465, JST ASPIRE JPMJAP2302, and JST ACT-X JPMJAX25CT. †Supported by JSPS JP25K24465 and JST ASPIRE JPMJAP2302.

## 1 Introduction

We study the _online coloring_ problem, in which vertices are revealed one by one. When a vertex arrives, we must assign it a color immediately, before the next vertex arrives, so that its color differs from the colors of all its previously revealed neighbors. See Figure 1 for an example. This is one of the most extensively studied problems in online algorithms, alongside the _k_-server problem, paging/caching, and online matching \[Alb03\].

### 1.1 Online Coloring

Online coloring is a classical problem for which natural algorithms are ineffective. The most intuitive strategy is _First-Fit_ \[GL88\], which always chooses the smallest available color. However, First-Fit can use _n/_2 colors even on an _n_-vertex bipartite graph, as shown in Figure 2 (such graphs are called crown graphs<sup>1</sup>). Accordingly, online coloring has been widely studied since the 1980s \[LST89\]. The best-known upper bounds on the competitive ratio are as follows: \(O(\frac{n}{logn})\) for randomized algorithms by Halldórsson (1997) \[Hal97\], and \(O(\frac{n}{loglogn})\) for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025) \[KYY25\]. In contrast, a lower bound of \(\Omega(\frac{n}{log^2n})\) is known due to Halldórsson and Szegedy (1994) \[HS94\].

Given these strong negative results, online coloring of _k_-colorable graphs for a fixed \(k\ge 2\) has received attention. For bipartite graphs (_k=_2), a deterministic algorithm by Lovász, Saks, and Trotter (1989) \[LST89\] achieves _O_(log_n_) colors. The situation becomes much harder for \(k\ge 3\): even for _k=_3, the best-known results are a randomized \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2})\)-color algorithm by Vishwanathan (1992) \[Vis92\] and a deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\)-color algorithm by Kierstead (1998) \[Kie98\]. For comparison, the best-known lower bound is \(\Omega(log^{k-1}n)\) colors \[Vis92\], leaving a substantial gap between the upper and lower bounds.

Online coloring is also studied for special graph classes, e.g., trees \[Bea76\], interval graphs \[KT81\], planar graphs \[Ira94\], bounded-treewidth graphs \[AS21\], and graphs of large odd girth \[YY26\]. See \[Kie05\] for a survey on online coloring.

## 1.2 The Random-Order Model

The _random-order model_, which assumes that the input order is chosen uniformly at random, is widely studied in the context of online algorithms. The most well-known problem is arguably the _secretary problem_, in which _n_ candidates arrive for a job interview in random order, and the interviewer must decide immediately after each interview whether to hire the candidate. Only one candidate can be hired overall. Thanks to random arrivals, the classical secretary algorithm [Lin61] selects the best candidate with probability at least \(\frac{1}{e}\approx 0.368\). In contrast, under an adversarial arrival order, no algorithm can guarantee a success probability greater than \(\frac{1}{n}\). The random-order model also leads to improved performance in many other online problems, including the following examples (see [GS21] for a survey):

• For the online bipartite matching problem, the optimal (tight) randomized competitive ratio is \(1-\frac{1}{e}\approx 0.632\) under adversarial arrivals [KVV90]. However, under the random-order model, an algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 0.696 [MY11].<tbc>

• For the online knapsack problem, no algorithm can achieve a bounded competitive ratio under adversarial arrivals. However, under the random-order model, an algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 0.153 [KK26].

### Online Coloring.

In online coloring with random arrivals, the given graph _G_=(_V,E_) is fixed, and the arrival order of the _n_ vertices is chosen uniformly at random from the _n_! possibilities, each with probability \(\frac{1}{n!}\). This setting has been particularly well-studied for First-Fit.

• For trees, First-Fit uses \(\Theta(\mathrm{log}n)\) colors under adversarial arrivals [Bea76; GL88], but it drops to \(\Theta(\frac{\mathrm{log}n}{\mathrm{loglog}n})\) colors in expectation under the random-order model [FGK+24; BGL+24].<tbc>

• For crown graphs (Figure 2), First-Fit uses _n/_2 colors under adversarial arrivals, but it drops to \(2.5+O(\frac{1}{n})\) colors in expectation under the random-order model [YXW+26].<tbc>

• For general bipartite graphs, it was conjectured that First-Fit only uses polylogarithmic number of colors in the random-order model [BGL+24], but it is claimed to be disproved; a very recent preprint shows a lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{1/2000})\) colors in expectation [LL26].

However, due to the inherent difficulty of online coloring, few studies have investigated random arrivals beyond First-Fit. In particular, it remained open whether algorithms for _k_-colorable graphs could be improved under the random-order model; for example, whether an \(O(n^{1/2-\varepsilon})\)-color algorithm exists for 3-colorable graphs, which would improve upon the result of [Vis92].

## 1.3 Our Contribution

In this paper, we show that the random-order model substantially improves the performance in online coloring: _k_-colorable graphs can be colored online with a _polylogarithmic_ number of colors for any constant _k_. Formally, we prove the following main theorem.

**Theorem 1.** _In the random-order model, when both n and k are known in advance, there exists a randomized online algorithm that colors any k-colorable n-vertex graph using O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) _colors in expectation._

This result significantly improves upon the previous \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1-\frac{1}{k-1}})\)-color bound [Vis92]. In addition, for all fixed \(k\ge 6\), our random-order result is better than the known lower bound of \(\Omega(log^{k-1}n)\) colors for adversarial arrivals [Vis92]. Therefore, we establish the _asymptotic separation_ between the random-order model and the adversarial-order model.

Moreover, assuming the result of the recent preprint [LL26], which claims that First-Fit uses expected \(\Omega(n^{1/2000})\) colors for some bipartite graphs under random arrivals (and hence, for every \(k\ge 2\), some _k_-colorable graphs), our algorithm asymptotically outperforms First-Fit for all \(k\ge 2\).

Furthermore, we obtain a competitive ratio of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\), as stated in the following theorem.

**Theorem 2.** _In the random-order model, when n is known in advance, there exists a randomized online algorithm that attains a competitive ratio of_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\).

Given the known lower bound of \(\Omega(\frac{n}{log^2n})\) on the competitive ratio for adversarial arrivals [HS94], this also establishes the _asymptotic separation_ between the random-order model and the adversarial-order model in terms of the competitive ratio. Note that our result assumes that _n_ is known in advance. This is a standard assumption in the random-order model; several previous studies [AJ21; AKL21; Lin61; SSZ25] also make the same assumption.

## 1.4 Online Algorithms vs. Approximation Algorithms

A broader question in theoretical computer science concerns the relationship between the _competitive ratio_ in online algorithms and the _approximation ratio_ in polynomial-time approximation algorithms. This topic is discussed in various studies [KKL07; MAS14]. In general, if an online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the hardness barrier for polynomial-time approximation algorithms, then it must run in super-polynomial time.

As a matter of fact, online algorithms can achieve better performance guarantees than approximation algorithms for some problems, although we did not find any references that explicitly mention this observation. The work of Rubinstein (2016) [Rub16] presents an _O_(log_n_)-competitive algorithm for the (maximum cardinality) secretary problem on a downward-closed set system. This immediately yields an _O_(log_n_)-competitive algorithm for "online maximum independent set" with random arrivals. In contrast, approximating (offline) maximum independent set within a factor of \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) is NP-hard for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), as shown by Zuckerman (2006) [Zuc06].

This paper gives an exponential-time \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\)-competitive algorithm for online coloring with random arrival order (Theorem 2), whereas approximating (offline) graph coloring within a factor of \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) is NP-hard for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) [Zuc06]. Therefore, we establish the _asymptotic separation_ between online and (deterministic or randomized) approximation algorithms in graph coloring,<tbc>

under the widely believed assumption that \(\text{NP}\unknown\in\text{BPP}\) [AB09]. We note that, although a graph coloring can be obtained by repeatedly choosing a maximum independent set among the uncolored vertices, Rubinstein’s algorithm [Rub16] does not directly imply an online coloring algorithm for random arrivals because the random arrival order on the uncolored vertices is not guaranteed.

**Remark 3.** _Since the approximation side allows randomized algorithms, including random-order processing, we regard this comparison as fair. Moreover, our result achieves O_(log<sup>4</sup>_n_) _colors for 3-colorable graphs; however, no polynomial-time algorithm that colors 3-colorable graphs with O(n_<sup>1/10</sup>) _colors is known at the time of writing._<sup>2</sup>

## 1.5 Overview of the Algorithm

In this subsection, we present an overview of our algorithm and the intuition behind using random arrival order. For simplicity, we consider the case _k=_3 here; the goal is to color a 3-colorable graph _G=(V,E_) online with _O_(log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors.

First, it suffices to devise an algorithm that colors the last _n/_2 vertices with _O_(log<sup>3</sup>_n_) colors, using information from the first _n/_2 vertices. If this can be done, we can color the entire graph with _O_(log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors by recursively applying the same algorithm to the first _n/_2 vertices (for example, we color the _n/_4+1_,...,n/_2-th vertices using information from the first _n/_4 vertices), using completely disjoint color sets for different levels of recursion. Here, we denote the set of the first _n/_2 vertices by _S_.

### The Benefit of Random Order.

The benefit of random arrival order is that \(S\subseteq V\) can be assumed to be chosen uniformly at random. Hence, we can assume that the two parts, _G[S_] and _G[V_\\_S_], have similar properties. For example, the sizes of maximum independent sets and the sizes of each color class in a 3-coloring \(\varphi:V\rightarrow\{1,2,3\}\) are very similar.

In particular, for a sufficiently large independent set \(I\subseteq V\) , the parts of _I_ that lie in _S_ and in _V_\\_S_ do not differ much in size, with a statistical error of only \(\pm\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\). Therefore, after the first _n/_2 vertices have arrived, if we "sample" an independent set \(I\subseteq S\) of _G[S_], then it is likely that _I_ can be "extended" to the vertices in _V_\\_S_ to the extent as large as _I_. This mechanism allows us to obtain a large independent set in _G[V_\\_S_] online.

### Hardcore Sampling and Extension.

After receiving all vertices in _S_, we sample an independent set \(I\subseteq S\) from the _hardcore model_ [DK25; Wei06] with parameter \(\lambda\approx\frac{1}{40lnn}\), where _I_ is chosen with probability proportional to \(\lambda^{|I|}\). As implied by the fact that a 3-colorable graph _G[S_] has an independent set of size at least |_S|/_3≈_n/_6, the expected size of _I_ is \(\Theta(\lambda n)=\Theta(\frac{n}{logn})\).

Then, the set of "eligible" vertices for extending the independent set _I_ toward _V_\\_S_ is \(J:=\{v\in V\backslash S:N_I(v)=\emptyset\}\), which is sufficiently large by the discussion above.<sup>3</sup> While _J_ itself may not be an independent set, it can be proven that _G[J_] most probably has maximum degree _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_). #### Covering _V_\\_S_ with Multiple Samples.

The issue is that, with a single independent set _I_, only a fraction of the vertices in _V_\\_S_ are colored. We address this issue by _carefully_ sampling a sequence of independent sets _I_<sub>1</sub>_,...,I<sub>r</sub>_ (\(I_r=\emptyset\)), where _r_ is most probably _O_(log_n_). We also maintain "bins" \(J_1,\dots,J_r\subseteq V\backslash S\) for the extension counterpart, initially empty.

For each arrival of \(v\in V\backslash S\), we find the smallest _i_ such that \(N_{I_i}(v)=\emptyset\), and put _v_ into _J<sub>i</sub>_. Then, we can prove that each _G[J<sub>i</sub>_] most probably has maximum degree _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_). Hence, by applying First-Fit to each of _G[J_<sub>1</sub>]_,...,G[J<sub>r</sub>_], using a separate set of colors for each bin, we can most probably color the entire _V_\\_S_ with \(r\cdot O(log^2n)=O(log^3n)\) colors.

## 2 Preliminaries

Before moving on to our algorithms, we present the required notation and definitions. First, we formally define online coloring with random arrival order. Then, we define First-Fit, the most straightforward strategy for online coloring.

## 3 Hardcore Model

In this section, we discuss the properties of randomly sampled independent sets. We sample independent sets using the _hardcore model_ \[DK25; Wei06\].

**Definition 7** (Hardcore Model)**.** _Given a graph G_=(_V,E), the hardcore model_ \(\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)\) _with parameter_ \(\lambda>0\) _is a probability distribution that chooses an independent set_ \(I\in\mathcal{I}(G)\) _with probability proportional to_ \(\lambda^{|I|}\)_. More precisely, define_

\(Z_\lambda(G):=\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}(G)}\lambda^{|I|}.\)

_Then, an independent set_ \(I\in\mathcal{I}(G)\) _is chosen with probability_ \(\frac{\lambda^{|I|}}{Z_\lambda(G)}\)_. See Figure 4 for an example._

Note that the case \(\lambda=1\) was already studied by Nilli (1988) \[Nil88\], who showed that the average size of independent sets for a _k_-colorable graph is \(\Omega(\frac{n}{klogk})\) and proved that this bound is tight. **Lemma 10.** _Let_ \(\lambda\in(0,1]\)_, and let G_=(_V,E_) _be a k-colorable graph. Then,_ \(\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[|I|]\ge\frac{\lambda}{3kln(3k)}|V|.\) _Proof._ First, the function \(f(x)=(\frac{1}{3k})^x\) is convex, so it follows from Jensen’s inequality that: \(\left(\frac{1}{3k}\right)^{\mathbb{E}[|I|]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{3k}\right)^{|I|}\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{Z_\lambda(G)}\cdot\left(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}(G)}\left(\frac{1}{3k}\right)^{|I|}\lambda^{|I|}\right)=\frac{Z_{\lambda/3k}(G)}{Z_\lambda(G)}\le\frac{(1+\lambda/3k)^{|V|}}{(1+\lambda)^{|V|/k}}\) The last inequality is due to Proposition 8. Therefore: \(\mathbb{E}[|I|]\ge-log_{3k}\frac{(1+\lambda/3k)^{|V|}}{(1+\lambda)^{|V|/k}}\)
\(=\frac{1}{ln(3k)}\left\{\frac{|V|}{k}ln(1+\lambda)-|V|ln\left(1+\frac{\lambda}{3k}\right)\right\}\)
\(\ge\frac{1}{ln(3k)}\left\{\frac{|V|}{k}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\lambda-|V|\cdot\frac{\lambda}{3k}\right\}=\frac{\lambda}{3kln(3k)}|V|\) The last inequality follows from \(\frac{2}{3}x\le ln(1+x)\le x\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\). □

## 3.3 The Neighborhood Structures We also investigate the structure surrounding a random independent set \(I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)\). In the following two lemmas, we analyze the expected size of \(I\cup N(I)\). **Lemma 11.** _Let_ \(\lambda>0\)_, and let G_=(_V,E_) _be a graph. Then,_ \(\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[|I|]=\lambda\cdot\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[|V\backslash(I\cup N(I))|].\) _Proof._ Fix \(v\in V\) . Let \(\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{in}=\{I\in\mathcal{I}:v\in I\}\), and \(\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{out}=\{I\in\mathcal{I}:v\in V\backslash(I\cup N(I))\}\). Then, the relationship \(\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{in}=\{I\cup\{v\}:I\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{out}\}\) holds (Figure 5), as shown below: • For every \(I\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{out}\), \(I\cup\{v\}\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{in}\) because \(I\cup\{v\}\) is an independent set due to \(v\notin I\cup N(I)\). • For every \(I\cup\{v\}\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{in}\), \(I\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{out}\) because _I_ is an independent set and \(v\notin N(I)\). Here, for each \(I\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{out}\), the probability that \(I\cup\{v\}\) is chosen is \(\lambda\) times the probability that _I_ is chosen. Therefore, \(\mathrm{Pr}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[I\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{in}]=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{Pr}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[I\in\mathcal{I}_v^\mathrm{out}](\forall v\in V)\)
\(\text{Equivalently,}\mathrm{Pr}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[v\in I]=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{Pr}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[v\in V\backslash(I\cup N(I))](\forall v\in V)\) Summing this equation over all \(v\in V\) , we have \(\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[|I|]=\lambda\cdot\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[|V\backslash(I\cup N(I))|]\) by linearity of expectation. □ **Lemma 12.** _Let_ \(\lambda\in(0,1]\)_, and let G_=(_V,E_) _be a k-colorable graph. Then,_ \(\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G)}[|I\cup N(I)|]\le\left(1-\frac{1}{3k\mathrm{ln}(3k)}\right)|V|.\) _Proof._ By Lemma 11, \(\mathbb{E}[|V\backslash(I\cup N(I))|]=\frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot\mathbb{E}[|I|]\). Thus, by Lemma 10, \(\mathbb{E}[|I\cup N(I)|]=|V|-\frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot\mathbb{E}[|I|]\)
\(\le|V|-\frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\lambda}{3k\mathrm{ln}(3k)}|V|=\left(1-\frac{1}{3k\mathrm{ln}(3k)}\right)|V|.\) □

## 4 The Algorithm

We present an algorithm that colors _k_-colorable graphs online with _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors in the random-order model. The intuition is already given in Subsection 1.5. Note that, in the subsequent sections, we use _G_=(_V,E_) to denote the current graph for the algorithm and _G_<sup>∗</sup>=(_V_<sup>∗</sup>_,E_<sup>∗</sup>) to denote the final graph, as in Definition 5.

### 4.1 Basic Strategy

We consider developing an algorithm that colors the last _n/_2 vertices using _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_) colors, given that the first _n/_2 vertices have already arrived and have been colored. If this can be done, we can recursively apply the same algorithm to the first _n/_2 vertices. Then, we can color the entire graph with _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors.

However, for convenience in the analysis, we do not exactly divide them into _n/_2 vertices each. Instead, we sample _m_ from a binomial distribution \(\mathsf{Binomial}(n,\frac{1}{2})\), and we color the last _n-m_ vertices, given that the first _m_ vertices have already arrived. We note that _m_ is very close to _n/_2 (with \(\pm\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) error), so this does not fundamentally change the algorithm. We use disjoint colors for the first _m_ vertices and the last _n-m_ vertices. Let _S_ be the set of the first _m_ vertices. Under this framework, \(S\subseteq V^*\) is uniformly distributed over the 2_<sup>n</sup>_ subsets of _V_<sup>∗</sup>, as shown below.

**Lemma 13.** _Let_ \(m\sim\mathsf{Binomial}(n,\frac{1}{2})\)_. Let S be the set of the first m vertices. Then, each subset of V_<sup>∗</sup> _appears as S with probability exactly_ 2<sup>-_n_</sup>.

_Proof._ The probability that |_S|=m_ is \(2^{-n}\cdot\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}\) by the binomial distribution. Also, there are \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}\) possible subsets of _V_<sup>∗</sup> with size _m_, and all of them have equal probabilities of appearing as _S_ because of the random-order model. Hence, Lemma 13 holds. □

### 4.2 Algorithm Details

Now, we consider an algorithm to color the last _n-m_ vertices _V_<sup>∗</sup>\\_S_. The algorithm consists of two phases: (1) the _learning phase_, which learns and extracts the structure of the first _m_ vertices, and (2) the _output phase_, which actually colors the last _n-m_ vertices by exploiting the learned structure. The two phases are described as follows.

#### (1) The Learning Phase.

The core idea is that, if we sample an independent set \(I\subseteq S\), many vertices in _V_<sup>∗</sup>\\_S_ are likely to have no neighbor in _I_ thanks to the random arrivals (Subsection 1.5). Such a set of vertices can be colored efficiently, as we prove in Section 5. However, a single sampled independent set _I_ does not cover all vertices in _V_<sup>∗</sup>\\_S_. Therefore, we need to sample multiple independent sets.

In the algorithm, we sample a sequence of independent sets _I_<sub>1</sub>_,I_<sub>2</sub>_,..._, each from a hierarchy \((S=)A_1\unknown A_2\unknown\cdots\) . We start with _A_<sub>1</sub>=_S_. For _i_=1,2_,..._ in this order, we sample an independent set _I<sub>i</sub>_ from \(\mathsf{IS}_\lambda(G[A_i])\), and then we let _A_<sub>_i_+1</sub>:=_N<sub>A<sub>i</sub></sub>(I<sub>i</sub>_). See Figure 6 for an example. Eventually, _I<sub>i</sub>_ becomes empty; we let _r_ be the first index such that \(I_r=\emptyset\). When coloring the remaining _n-m_ vertices, we use independent sets _I_<sub>1</sub>_,...,I<sub>r</sub>_. It can be proven that _r=O(k_log_k_log_n_) with high probability (Lemma 16), regardless of the value of the parameter \(\lambda\in(0,1]\).

#### (2) The Output Phase.

Next, we color the remaining _n-m_ vertices. Here, we maintain bins \(J_1,\dots,J_r\subseteq V^*\backslash S\), initially empty, which correspond to _I_<sub>1</sub>_,...,I<sub>r</sub>_, respectively.

When a vertex \(v\in V^*\backslash S\) arrives, we put _v_ into _J<sub>i</sub>_ for the smallest _i_ such that \(N_{I_i}(v)=\emptyset\). Such an _i_ must exist because \(I_r=\emptyset\). Although _J<sub>i</sub>_ is not necessarily an independent set, it can be proven that the maximum degree of _G_<sup>∗</sup>\[_J<sub>i</sub>_\] is \(O((k\mathrm{log}n)/\lambda)\) with high probability in the range of \(i\le\frac{1}{\lambda}\) (Lemma 21). Hence, with the parameter setting

\(\lambda:=\frac{1}{6k\mathrm{ln}(3k)\mathrm{ln}n+2},\)

_G_<sup>∗</sup>\[_J_<sub>1</sub>\]_,...,G_<sup>∗</sup>\[_J<sub>r</sub>_\] all have maximum degrees _O(k_<sup>2</sup>log_k_log<sup>2</sup>_n_) with high probability (Lemma 22). Therefore, we can use the First-Fit algorithm to color each vertex of _G_<sup>∗</sup>\[_J<sub>i</sub>_\]. We use disjoint sets of colors for bins _J_<sub>1</sub>_,...,J<sub>r</sub>_.

#### Overall Algorithm.

The pseudocode for the entire algorithm is presented in Algorithm 1. With high probability, we use _O(k_<sup>2</sup>log_k_log<sup>2</sup>_n_) colors for each _J<sub>i</sub>_, and _r=O(k_log_k_log_n_). Therefore, we use _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_) colors in expectation for the last _n-m_ vertices (Lemma 23). We analyze the algorithm’s performance in detail in the next section.

**Remark 14.** _The runtime of Algorithm 1 is unbounded for the scenario where m=n is chosen every time. However, if m=n, the only thing that happens is a call to the identical procedure COLORING<sub>k</sub>(n). Therefore, the outcome of Algorithm 1 remains the same if we choose m from the distribution that excludes m=n, i.e., each m_=0_,...,n_-1 _is chosen with probability_ \(\frac{1}{2^n-1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}\)_; this change makes its runtime bounded. Note that r is also bounded; we will prove_ \(r\le n+1\) _in Lemma 15. Nevertheless, this algorithm runs in exponential time, because sampling an independent set from_ \(\mathsf{I}\mathsf{S}_\lambda(G[A_r])\) _takes exponential time._

**Lemma 20.** _Let_ \(\lambda\in(0,1]\) _be the parameter of the hardcore model. Suppose G_<sup>∗</sup>=(_V_<sup>∗</sup>_,E_<sup>∗</sup>) _is a fixed k-colorable graph. For every vertex_ \(v\in V^*\) _and every positive integer_ \(t\le\frac{1}{\lambda}\),

\(Pr\left[v\in J_t\text{\textit{and}}|N(v)\cap J_t|\ge\frac{10klnn}{\lambda}\right]\le\frac{1}{n^3}.\) (3)

_Proof._ First, for every positive integer \(t\le\frac{1}{\lambda}\), we have

\(\frac{\lambda}{(1+\lambda)^t}\ge\frac{\lambda}{(1+\lambda)^{1/\lambda}}\ge\frac{\lambda}{e}.\)

Therefore, Lemma 19 implies that the following inequality also holds for \(t\le\frac{1}{\lambda}\):

\(\mathbb{E}\left[(1+\lambda/e)^{|N(v)\cap J_t|/k}\text{if}v\in J_t\text{, otherwise}0\right]\le 1.\) (4)

By Markov’s inequality, Equation 4 implies \(Pr[v\in J_t\text{and}(1+\lambda/e)^{|N(v)\cap J_t|/k}\ge n^3]\le\frac{1}{n^3}\). By taking the logarithm of both sides, the condition above becomes

\(|N(v)\cap J_t|\ge\frac{3klnn}{ln(1+\lambda/e)}.\) (5)

Here,

\(\frac{3klnn}{ln(1+\lambda/e)}\le\frac{3klnn}{(3/10)\cdot\lambda}=\frac{10klnn}{\lambda}.\) (6)

This is due to \(ln(1+x/e)\ge\frac{3}{10}x\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\). Therefore, combining Equation 5 and Equation 6, the probability that \(v\in J_t\) and \(|N(v)\cap J_t|\ge\frac{10klnn}{\lambda}\) is at most \(\frac{1}{n^3}\). □

## 5.3 The Grand Finale

Finally, we analyze the total number of colors used in Algorithm 1.

**Lemma 23.** _In Algorithm 1, the number of colors used for V_<sup>∗</sup>\\_S is O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_) _in expectation._

_Proof._ If the maximum degrees in _G_\[_J_<sub>1</sub>\]_,...,G_\[_J<sub>r</sub>_\] are at most \(\Delta\), then First-Fit uses at most \(\Delta+1\) colors, resulting in at most \(r(\Delta+1)\) colors for the entire _V_<sup>∗</sup>\\_S_. Therefore, by Lemma 16, Lemma 22, and the union bound, we use at most \(O(k\mathrm{log}k\mathrm{log}n)\cdot O(k^2\mathrm{log}k\mathrm{log}^2n)=O(k^3\mathrm{log}^2k\mathrm{log}^3n)\) colors with probability at least \(1-\frac{4}{n}\). In the remaining case, which occurs with probability at most \(\frac{4}{n}\), we may use up to _n_ colors, but this is negligible. □

**Lemma 24.** _The number of calls to_ \(\mathsf{COLORING}_k(\cdot)\) _in Algorithm 1 is at most_ 2log<sub>2</sub>_n_+1 _with probability at least_ \(1-\frac{1}{n}\).

_Proof._ By Lemma 13, each vertex \(v\in V^*\) is put into _S_, i.e., colored in the recursion, with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Hence, each vertex \(v\in V^*\) goes down for at least 2log<sub>2</sub>_n_ recursions with probability at most \(2^{-2\mathrm{log}_2n}=\frac{1}{n^2}\). If this does not happen for any \(v\in V^*\), then the recursion depth in Algorithm 1 is at most 2log<sub>2</sub>_n_. By the union bound, this occurs with probability at least \(1-\frac{1}{n^2}\cdot|V^*|=1-\frac{1}{n}\). □

We are now ready to prove our main theorem, which shows that Algorithm 1 uses at most _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors in expectation.

**Theorem 1** (restated)**.** _In the random-order model, when both n and k are known in advance, there exists a randomized online algorithm that colors any k-colorable n-vertex graph using O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) _colors in expectation._

_Proof._ For each call to \(\mathsf{COLORING}_k(\cdot)\), we use _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_) colors in expectation, due to Lemma 23. Note that we can assume random arrivals in each call to \(\mathsf{COLORING}_k(m)\), because _m_ does not depend on the graph structure (i.e., it depends only on random choices), and the probability of this event does not change by shuffling the order of the first _m_ vertices, due to the random-order assumption in the original graph _G_<sup>∗</sup>.

Hence, across the shallowest \(\lfloor 2\mathrm{log}_2n+1\rfloor\) calls to \(\mathsf{COLORING}_k(\cdot)\) (or all calls if there are fewer), we use _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors in expectation. If there are more than 2log<sub>2</sub>_n_+1 calls, at most _n_ colors may be used, but this probability is at most \(\frac{1}{n}\) (Lemma 24), so this is negligible. □

## 6 The Competitive Ratio

We consider online coloring with random arrivals for general graphs. In online coloring, a lower bound of \(\Omega(\frac{n}{\mathrm{log}^2n})\) on the competitive ratio is known for both deterministic and randomized algorithms \[HS94\]. However, with the random-order model, we can do better.

**Theorem 2** (restated)**.** _In the random-order model, when n is known in advance, there exists a randomized online algorithm that attains a competitive ratio of_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\).

_Proof._ The idea is to simulate the behavior of Algorithm 1 for 2_<sup>q</sup>_-colorable graphs, COLORING<sub>2_<sup>q</sup>_</sub>(_n_), on the same input graph _G_, for each \(q=0,1,\dots,\lceil\mathrm{log}_2n\rceil\) in parallel processes. We assume disjoint sets of colors for different processes. For each arrival of vertex \(v\in V\) , we color _v_ using the color selected by the process that has used the fewest colors so far.

We now analyze the number of colors used. Let \(q^*:=\lceil\mathrm{log}_2\chi(G^*)\rceil\). Since _G_<sup>∗</sup> is 2_<sup>q</sup>_<sup>∗</sup>-colorable, by Theorem 1, the number of colors used by the process with _q=q_<sup>∗</sup>, denoted by _c_<sub>_q_<sup>∗</sup></sub>, satisfies

\(\mathbb{E}[c_{q^*}]=O((2^{q^*})^3\mathrm{log}^2(2^{q^*})\mathrm{log}^4n)=O(\chi(G^*)^3\mathrm{log}^2\chi(G^*)\mathrm{log}^4n).\)

Moreover, for each process, at most _c_<sub>_q_<sup>∗</sup></sub> colors are used in the _actual_ online coloring, so the number of colors used overall is at most \(c_{q^*}(\lceil\mathrm{log}_2n\rceil+1)\). Therefore, this algorithm uses \(O(\chi(G^*)^3\mathrm{log}^2\chi(G^*)\mathrm{log}^5n)\) colors in expectation. Also, it is obvious that we use at most _n_ colors. Thus, we attain a competitive ratio of _O(n_<sup>2/3</sup>log<sup>7/3</sup>_n_), with the worst-case bound attained when \(\chi(G^*)=\Theta(\frac{n^{1/3}}{\mathrm{log}^{7/3}n})\). □

## 7 Conclusion

In this paper, we presented an algorithm for online coloring with random arrivals that uses _O(k_<sup>3</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_k_log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors for _k_-colorable graphs. For online coloring as a whole, we improved the performance for the case _k=_3 from \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2})\) colors \[Vis92\] to _O_(log<sup>4</sup>_n_) colors. We also achieved a competitive ratio of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})\), which is better than the conventional lower bound \(\Omega(\frac{n}{\mathrm{log}^2n})\) \[HS94\] and is better than an \(\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})\) inapproximability bound for graph coloring \[Zuc06\]. These results demonstrate that the random-order model unlocks new possibilities for improving the performance of online coloring algorithms. It is now natural to pose the following conjectures.

**Conjecture 25.** _In the random-order model, when both n and k are known in advance, there exists a randomized online algorithm that colors any k-colorable n-vertex graph using O(k_log_n_) _colors in expectation._

**Conjecture 26.** _In the random-order model, when n is known in advance, there exists a randomized online algorithm that attains a competitive ratio of O_(log_n)._

Finally, a limitation of our result is that it relies on the random-order model and does not extend to adversarial arrivals. It is natural to ask whether the following conjecture holds.

**Conjecture 27.** _For any constant_ \(k\ge 3\)_, there exists a (randomized) online algorithm for coloring k-colorable graphs with n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> _colors, even without assuming random arrivals._
